chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 3 of 6): the poet asks to be freed from infatuation with women and courtesans who seek money, from the body of the five elements, from the kin who crowd the deathbed, and from praising petty patrons, and asks for the feet, for daily worship and service, and for Murugan to face Death on his behalf; he also scorns poets who sing love-sickness without naming Senthil.
structure_note: Courtesan and lust songs (51 to 54, 56 to 58, 65); the body and death (61, 63); the poet's craft, against praising men (55, 60) and against love poems that leave out Senthil (64); a doctrinal question in Saiva terms (59); and a song of longing to see Murugan's form (62). 57 and 58 share a run of epithets ending -க்கார.

51.reading: In clipped rhythm the poet speaks of women with breasts, cloud-dark hair, eyes like konrai arrows and carp and parrot speech, who meet men at the ends of streets, and asks not to be entangled with them but to have Murugan set his feet on his head. The praise is obscure: it seems to tell of the demon who left his army and fled into the sea, and names the lord at Senthil who keeps tenderness in his heart.
51.nuance: என்றன் தலையில் சந்தப் பதம் வைத்தருள்வாயே: the feet placed on the head, the gesture of the guru's initiation. சந்தப்படி may also mean 'in the rhythm of the song'. Most of the praise cannot be divided with confidence.

52.reading: The poet describes himself in a long series of names: one who drinks women's lips, wounded by their nails, a sinner, without knowledge, path or virtue, a man who never melts with love crying 'Senthil' and has given nothing, and asks whether Murugan will not give him his two small lotus feet with love. The praise names the peacock that tears the serpent, the vel that splits the demons joint by joint, and Siva the eight-qualitied, formless ancient Lord who burnt the three cities, with Ganga, konrai and crescent in his hair and the bull for his mount; and Murugan as the master of Tamil to whom Uma gave her breast, whom Sankara worships.
52.nuance: கவுரி உமை கொங்கை தந்து அன்புறும் தமிழ் விரக: the Tamil master who drank Uma's breast milk is Sambandar's story, here given to Murugan. எண்குணன் for Siva is the Kural's epithet for the Lord. Several words in the first half (செஞ்செநீடும், அண்டுஞ்சகன்) are unclear.

53.reading: The poet asks not to be dazzled by women's breasts with sandal, kumkum and ornaments and their hair with water-lily garlands, but to sing daily 'Lord of the gods, namo nama; my Lord, namo nama; lover of the bangled one, namo nama', do proper worship with love and not waste his days. The praise names the Goddess, who danced like a spinning top, queen of ghouls, Kali, Yogini, holding the trident, who saw the war with drink-sodden Sura and blessed her son with the victorious vel, and Murugan as lord of Vayalur, Visakha, and the life of Senthil who saves the poet.
53.nuance: The plea contains its own litany: the நமோநம lines are the praise the poet asks to be able to sing. The vel is given by the Goddess (எம்புதல்வா வாழி வாழி எனும்படி வீறான வேல்தர), which ties it to Shakti. Vayalur, another shrine, is named among the epithets.

54.reading: The poet calls himself a dog who drank the lips of women with breasts like a killer elephant's temples and melted in infatuation, and asks whether, with the cares that destroy him ended and the eye of grace on him, he will hold Murugan's flower feet in mind and come to cling to him. The praise names the child of red words graced by Siva whose bow is the northern mountain, the vel that killed the demon from the sea, the lover of the hunter girl and the rider of the emerald peacock.
54.nuance: நின் பற்று அடைவேனோ: the plea is for attachment, but attachment to the Lord, after attachment to women. செஞ்சொல் சிறுபாலா may point to Sambandar, again identified with Murugan, but that is uncertain.

55.reading: The poet asks not to wander praising women's conch-necks, coral mouths, pearl teeth and mountain breasts, nor to go to the men of the world telling them like a mother 'you are the noble Vel, you are the golden cloud of red hands', but, his sorrow and disease scattered, to say one word of service: 'good Kanda Vel'. The praise names Siva who took the poison and gave the gods nectar and dances in the great hall, before whom red-eyed Vishnu won the bright discus, and Murugan the red-Tamil lord of Senthil whom that moon-crowned Siva loves.
55.nuance: The patron is flattered as Murugan himself (துங்கவேள்) and as a cloud for his giving: the poet asks to keep those names for the Lord alone. செங்கண்மால் பங்கயக் கண் ... கதிராழி appears to be Vishnu offering his lotus eye to Siva and receiving the discus, though the line is compressed.

56.reading: The poet calls himself a deceiver without shame, his heart full of agitation, puffed with the pomp of sandal and kumkum, and asks not to suffer in vain from the body's infatuation with women's breasts, but that Guha come with the splendour of his own form and rule him with love. The praise names the son of the Ganga-bearing lord, Kandha, who saved Indra's worlds from trembling, the hero of Indra's cause, the vel that killed Sura, and the lord at Senthil whom Vishnu and Brahma worship.
56.nuance: நின் சொரூப ப்ரகாசம் கொடே வந்து: the plea asks for the Lord's own form shining, a vision rather than a gift. The opening (சங்கைதான் ஒன்றுதான் இன்றியே) could mean without doubt or without shame, and the self-description is uncertain.

57.reading: The poet heaps comparisons on women's eyes, the seven roaring seas, honey, arrows, the shakti spear, the mango slice, the lily, lotus, poison and the leaping fish, and on their breasts, like a rutting elephant's temples, hung with pearls; he asks when, the delusion laid on them gone, Murugan will come on his diamond peacock for this poor servant to do him devotion. The praise is a chain of epithets ending -க்கார: holder of the vel in twelve hands, lord of the devotees' hymns, lover of the hunter girl, scourge of the demons, protector of the good, speaker of words that free devotees, expert in the three Tamils, lord at sea-girt Senthil.
57.nuance: The plea is a catalogue: piling the conventional comparisons is the infatuation itself, which the poet then asks to leave (வைத்த கொடிதான மயல் விட்டு). அடியார்கள் முத்திபெற வேசொல் வசனக்கார: Murugan is the one whose word gives release to devotees.

58.reading: The poet describes women scented with sandal, civet, camphor, kumkum and musk, in silk and diamonds, who seek money with great desire, cruel and deceitful at heart, whose glance of feigned longing withers his mind, and asks when Murugan will think to come and take him into service. The praise, again a chain of -க்கார epithets, names the guardian of Indra's city, the rider of the peacock, the ever-young, the lover of the hunter girl, Uma's son, the master of the four kinds of verse, the strength of the vel, the one easy for devotees, the glory of mantra teaching, at Senthil.
58.nuance: பொருள் தேடுமதி நிட்டூர வஞ்சக விசார இதய: money-seeking, cruel and deceitful hearts, the courtesan named by her motive. நாலுகவிதைக்கார, master of the four kinds of poetry, and மந்த்ர உபதேச மகிமைக்கார, glory of teaching the mantra, make Murugan both poet and guru.

59.reading: Rather than a plea, the poet asks a question: why do some, without loving the lotus feet the endless Vedas proclaim and without care for virtue, waste away in lust, anger and greed, in the changes of the elements, in the body of maya, in the bonds of soul and fetter? The praise names the warrior of the kadamba on the blue-necked peacock, whose war raised dust from Meru, son of the Mother who gives Sivaloka to those who keep the fire rite, the master who taught the way of yoga, lord of the silent gods.
59.nuance: The vocabulary is Saiva Siddhanta: பசு பாசம், மாயாகாயம், and the three faults காம க்ரோத லோப. The song asks a question (அது என்கொலோ தான்) instead of confessing. ஓமத் தீ வழுவார்கட்கு ஊர் சிவலோகத்தே தரு names the fire rite as a path to Sivaloka. ஊமைத் தேவர்கள் is unclear.

60.reading: The poet speaks of craving women with fragrant hair and golden breasts, joining them and leaving mantra, faith and prayer, and asks whether, ceasing to praise impure fools who wander the earth deceiving, he will adorn himself with Murugan's flower feet and worship. The praise is given in drum syllables for the dancing peacock and names the vel that destroyed the demons, the son of the mountain's daughter, and the lover of the hunter girl, at Senthil.
60.nuance: புநிதமிலி மாந்தர் தங்கள் புகழ்பகர்தல் நீங்கி: the poet gives up praising patrons, as in 55. The lines on studying Sangam Tamil poems (தாந்த்ரி சங்கத் தமிழ் பனுவல் ஆய்ந்து) may describe the poet himself or the men he praised; the reference is unclear.

61.reading: The poet calls himself a dog whose heart is set on women with cloud-dark hair full of honey and bees, and asks Murugan to come and give his golden feet before this false hut of earth, water, fire, wind and sky falls apart and goes to the harsh burning ground. The praise names Kumaresa who killed famous Sura, the lord of the fragrant hill where bees sing, and Kandha the son at Senthil.
61.nuance: மண் தோயம் தீ மென்கால் விண் தோய் வண் காயம் பொய்க் குடில்: the body is a false hut of the five elements, which come apart at death. Parts of the praise (கண்டா கும்பால் உண்டாய்) are unclear.

62.reading: The poet asks whether Murugan will not appear before him, so that his eyes are cooled, with anklets and bells ringing, as when he once danced with joy and embraced his father, with kadamba, crowns, lotus hands, vel, eyes and faces. The praise names the form that grew like a golden mountain to fill the worlds in battle until even Brahma's father (Vishnu) was amazed, the dance he dances at Senthil and before the poet himself, and the lord whom Agastya worships.
62.nuance: There is no confession here, only longing for sight (கண்குளிர என்றன்முன் சந்தியாவோ). செந்திலிலும் என்றன் முன் கொஞ்சி நடனங் கொளும்: the poet says Murugan dances before him, a claim of vision. The cosmic form (பொன்கிரியெனச் சிறந்து எங்கினும் வளர்ந்து) is Murugan's, not Vishnu's.

63.reading: The poet lists the kin who gather at death, mothers who fed and stroked him, brothers, servants, sisters, nephews, sons and wives, with their claims, and asks that when Death himself comes pressing on a buffalo, Murugan come on the strong peacock saying 'fear not' and tell that Death, 'Kandha says this man is our devotee'. The praise names the warrior whose peacock delights Uma, and the lord at Senthil of Siva who wears the moon, the serpent and the river.
63.nuance: அந்த மறலியொடு கந்த மனிதன் நமது அன்பன் என மொழிய: the plea is not only for Murugan to come but for him to speak to Death and claim the man as his own. The kin are pictured with the debts and claims they bring (கடனுதவு), so they offer no help.

64.reading: The poet scorns some who sit singing a few poor poems about a girl whose garment slips, who pines struck by Kama's arrows and is bewildered by the little southern breeze and burnt by the crescent, and do not know to speak of Thiruchendur and be saved. The praise names Murugan the guru who gave grace both to Siva, whose feet and crown Vishnu, Brahma and the Vedas could not know, and to the sage Agastya, and the lord who destroyed the demon's kin.
64.nuance: The love-sickness of the girl, with Kama's arrow, the south wind and the crescent, is the stock of akam verse; the complaint is against poems that spend these devices without naming the shrine. அரற்கும் ... கும்பநன் முநிக்கும் க்ருபை வரிக்கும் குருபர: Murugan as teacher both of Siva and of Agastya.

65.reading: The poet asks not to go near the agitation of women, which leaves the body wasted and suffering and love and goodness forgotten, but to be given the lotus feet the gods worship, so he may cry 'refuge' and do service forever. The praise names the younger one who, seeing the feet of the hunter girl who shares his side, cried 'refuge', stood behind her and bowed, and the lord at Senthil where valampuri conches throng the golden shore.
65.nuance: தஞ்சம் is said twice: the poet asks to cry 'refuge' at the Lord's feet, and the praise has the Lord crying 'refuge' at Valli's feet and bowing (கும்பிடும்). The devotee's surrender is mirrored in the god's surrender to his beloved.

links.note: The Kural bids one cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, to be free of all other clinging; 54 asks, after confessing his infatuation, to attain clinging to Murugan (நின் பற்று அடைவேனோ).

Both name the Lord the eight-qualitied (எண்குணத்தான், எண்குணன்): the Kural makes the head that does not bow to his feet useless; in 52 the eight-qualitied Siva is himself the one who bows, worshipping Murugan.

Both list the conventional comparisons for a woman's eyes, the carp, the lily, the spear. The Naladiyar names them as the talk of blind petty men to be ignored; 57 piles them up as the delusion that holds the poet, then asks to be freed of it.

The two songs are built alike: a confession that catalogues women's adornments, then a praise made of a chain of epithets ending -க்கார, each naming one role of Murugan. Read together they show the formula at work.
Tirumular warns against withering in praise of petty men for their wealth and bids one praise the Lord instead; 60 asks to give up praising impure men and to worship Murugan's feet.
Both quote the patron's flattery, the giver called a cloud and a lord of red or lotus hands. In 15 the poet confesses having begged so; in 55 he asks to keep such names for Murugan alone.

64 scorns poets who sing a girl's love-sickness, with Kama's arrows, the south wind and the crescent, without naming Thiruchendur; 24 uses the same devices, but for a girl in love with the lord of Senthil. The scorn falls on poems that leave out the shrine, not on the akam convention itself.
46 asks Murugan to come on the peacock when Death's messengers drag the poet off; 63 asks further that he speak to Death and claim the man as his own devotee.

source_issues: Song 53: corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 21), probably வயலூரா (Vayalur); flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS.
Song 57: corrupt character in வச்சிரகி஡ணடநிகர் (line 9), probably வச்சிர கிரீட நிகர் with ஡ண for ரீ; flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS.
Song 59: corrupt character in நீலக்஡ணபகலாபத் (line 11), probably நீலக்ரீப கலாப ('blue-necked, plumed') with ஡ண for ரீ; flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS.
Song 56: unflagged garble செர்ரு பம் (line 7), probably சொரூபம்.
